analysis.one_liner: Bars leasing federal land for oil and gas when it has little realistic chance of producing.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had no cosponsors and a single Senate hearing, died in the Energy and Natural Resources Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law lets the Interior Department offer public land for oil and gas leasing even when the land has little or no realistic chance of ever producing oil or gas. Companies can cheaply lock up those parcels, which taxpayer money then pays to administer, and the leases block other uses like grazing and recreation. This bill would require up-to-date government assessments of each parcel's actual oil and gas potential before leasing, and would bar leasing land rated as low- or no-potential except in narrow cases (like land next to a producing well) or through a strict public-interest variance with public comment. The bill never got a vote: after introduction it was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, received one subcommittee hearing, and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently fund issuing and managing speculative leases on land that rarely produces oil and brings in minimal revenue [S3]. Recreation, grazing, and conservation users of public land also gain, since dormant low-potential leases tie up land that could support those uses [S3].

how_it_helps.text: It would bar the government from offering for lease federal land that government analysis has rated as having low or no realistic potential to produce oil or gas, unless a narrow exception or a formal public-interest variance applies [S3].
It would require up-to-date, map-published assessments of oil and gas potential, with public notice and comment, before land is made available for leasing [S3].

It would limit speculation by allowing a company to lease low-potential land only through a stringent variance process — at most one per company per five years — with public review and the applicant bearing the burden of proof [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies that cheaply acquire low-potential federal parcels for speculation would lose that opportunity; the Interior Department would bear new analysis and update obligations before leasing [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill would add new analysis, public-comment periods, and update cycles before any leasing, which would slow the leasing process and add administrative work for the Bureau of Land Management [S2, S3].

Supporters of expanded energy production would argue that restricting which federal acres can be offered could shrink future supply, even though the bill's findings state the change is not detrimental to U.S. energy security [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real but modest: it targets a genuine waste — public land leased for near-minimum bids that rarely produces oil — and frees that land for grazing, recreation, and wildlife [S3]. The costs are small for the public, but the bill would add analysis and paperwork to federal leasing and could slow lease offerings, which oil and gas companies and some energy-security-minded lawmakers would call an unnecessary constraint [S2]. Since land with real development potential would still be leasable, the economic cost is likely limited to the speculative end of the market.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, and got one subcommittee hearing; the committee never sent it to the Senate floor, and the Congress ended without a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto introduced the bill on May 16, 2023 [S1, S2].
The Senate referred it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee; the only further action in the entire Congress was a single subcommittee hearing on public lands in July 2023 [S5].
The full committee never voted on the bill, so the Senate never debated or voted on it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies keep the status quo: the federal government continues to offer low-potential land for cheap speculative leases.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies, on the status quo

for.name: Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave it its only congressional-floor action: introduction and referral.

for.name: Senate Subcommittee on Public Lands, Forests, and Mining
for.role: Subcommittee of the Energy and Natural Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the bill in July 2023, its only committee consideration.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee, keeping it from a Senate floor vote.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.role: Industry opposing restrictions on federal leasing
against.what_they_did: Industry interests generally oppose restrictions on federal oil and gas leasing availability; no industry action on this bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew a vote or a single cosponsor from either party, so its partisan shape was never tested; it originated with a Democrat on a committee with no markup record.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies seeking federal leases
industries.note: Companies would lose the ability to cheaply acquire low-potential federal parcels for speculation, and would face a stricter, slower leasing process with public review and a variance bottleneck [S3]. Companies leasing genuinely promising land near existing wells could continue under the drainage exception [S3].

The Bureau of Land Management would gain new mandatory assessment, mapping, and public-comment duties before offering land, redirecting staff resources; the bill frames this as freeing resources currently wasted managing speculative leases [S3].

industries.industry: Recreation, grazing, and conservation users of public land
industries.note: Land currently locked up by dormant low-potential leases would stay open for grazing, recreation, wildlife, and other multiple uses the leases currently crowd out [S3].
